parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: power as rate of energy transfer
hints: Hint 1: Think about what power tells you about how quickly an engine or a person gets a job done, not just how much energy is involved.
parts.proper_answer: Power is the work done per unit time (rate of doing work).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Power Really Means**
Think of two identical aircraft engines where one climbs faster. Both do the same work to gain height, but the faster one is more powerful. So power links work and how quickly it is done: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Step 2: **Exact Definition**
Power is defined as the rate at which work is done, or work done divided by time taken. Unit is watt ($\text{W}$) which is $\text{J s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about why a raised mass has the ability to do work if released - what feature of its situation gives it stored energy?
parts.proper_answer: Energy of a mass due to its position in a gravitational field.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stored Energy From Position**
When you lift something up, you do work against gravity and that work is stored. It can be released as kinetic energy if the object falls. That stored ability to do work is what we call potential energy.

Step 2: **Exact Meaning**
Gravitational potential energy is the energy possessed by a mass because of its position in a gravitational field.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 3.1 and notice the thrust force acts along the same line as the velocity of 45 m s-1. Think about how power relates to a force pushing something that is already moving.
Hint 2: Use the force-velocity form for power when force and velocity are parallel, then substitute $F = 2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$ and $v = 45 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Power When Pushing a Moving Object**
You know power is work per time. Work is $F \times d$, so power is $F \times d/t$. But $d/t$ is velocity when force is in the direction of motion. That gives a very handy shortcut for engines and motors.

Step 2: **Apply to the Thrust**
Here thrust and velocity are parallel, so: $$P = Fv$$ $$P = (2.0 \times 10^3) \times 45$$ $$P = 9.0 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: energy conservation and work against resistance
hints: Hint 1: Start by sorting out the time and the two different motions - motion along the flight path at 45 m s-1 and vertical rise at 3.3 m s-1. Convert 3.0 minutes to seconds first.
Hint 2: For part 1, think about linking the power you just found to total energy supplied in the full time interval, or force times total distance along the path.
Hint 3: For part 2, focus only on the vertical gain. Think about which mass, which g and which vertical height change determine the stored gravitational energy.
Hint 4: For part 3, think about energy accounting - the thrust supplies energy, some is stored as gravitational potential, the rest must go elsewhere.
Hint 5: Check units and significant figures: work in joules from power in watts times time in seconds, and $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ with $\Delta h$ = vertical speed x time.
parts.proper_answer: 1. $W = 1.6 \times 10^7 \text{ J}$. 2. $\Delta E_p = 7.0 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$. 3. Work against air resistance $= 9.0 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Out the Time**
Always work in SI units. $$t = 3.0 \text{ min} = 3.0 \times 60 = 180 \text{ s}$$ Keep this for all three calculations.

Step 2: **1. Total Work From Thrust**
Power is energy per second, so total work is power x time. Using your $9.0 \times 10^4 \text{ W}$: $$W = Pt = 9.0 \times 10^4 \times 180$$ $$W = 1.62 \times 10^7 \text{ J} \approx 1.6 \times 10^7 \text{ J}$$ This is the same as $F \times (v t)$ along the path.

Step 3: **2. Gain in Gravitational Potential Energy**
Only vertical height counts for $mgh$. Vertical rise rate is $3.3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so: $$\Delta h = 3.3 \times 180 = 594 \text{ m}$$ Then: $$(\Delta E_p) = mg\Delta h = 1200 \times 9.81 \times 594$$ $$(\Delta E_p) \approx 7.0 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$$ Notice this is less than half the work supplied.

Step 4: **3. What Is Left Over?**
Energy cannot disappear. Thrust work goes into gravitational store plus work done against air resistance (which becomes heat and kinetic energy of air). Since speed is constant there is no change in kinetic energy: $$W_{resistance} = W_{thrust} - \Delta E_p$$ $$W_{resistance} = 1.6 \times 10^7 - 7.0 \times 10^6 \approx 9.0 \times 10^6 \text{ J}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the work against resistance you just found is linked to an average resistive force acting over the total distance travelled along the flight path in 180 s.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From Work Back to Force**
Work is force times distance in the direction of the force. The resistive force opposes motion along the path, so the work against it is $F \times d$ where $d$ is distance along the path.

Step 2: **Calculate Distance Then Force**
Distance along path: $$d = vt = 45 \times 180 = 8100 \text{ m}$$ Then: $$F = \frac{W}{d} = \frac{9.0 \times 10^6}{8100} \approx 1.1 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$$

parts.label: (b)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the motion described - constant velocity upwards along a straight path. Recall what Newton's first law says about resultant force when velocity is unchanged.
Hint 2: Connect zero resultant force to the formal meaning of equilibrium for a moving object.
parts.proper_answer: Yes, in equilibrium. Velocity is constant so acceleration is zero, hence resultant force is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Constant Velocity Means No Acceleration**
The aircraft climbs with constant velocity of $45 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ along a straight line. Constant velocity means zero acceleration. By $F = ma$, zero acceleration must mean zero resultant force.

Step 2: **Why This Is Equilibrium**
Equilibrium does not mean at rest, it means no resultant force or torque. Thrust, weight, lift and air resistance all balance out to give zero net force, so the aircraft is in equilibrium despite moving.
